title: Payments Company
difficulty_source_label: Overall 2, Quant 2, Creativity 1 (1-3 scale); Quant Level - MEDIUM
fit_question: Are you applying to all consulting firms, and why or why not? Alternatively, explain why the interviewer should hire you over your peers.
prompt: PayCo is a global credit-card company with more than $5B of revenue in 2010. It developed proprietary TAP contactless technology for cash-dominated transit systems such as subways, trains, buses, and taxis. Develop the business case for commercialization: which market and transit vertical should PayCo target first, will TAP break even in less than five years, and should PayCo pursue commercialization?

clarifying_info.answer: Contactless tap-and-go payment is increasingly used at fast-food restaurants and convenience stores.
PayCo wants to use contactless payments to drive top-line growth by entering the transit vertical.
Transit authorities may adopt TAP or retain their existing fare-collection systems.
The broader engagement covers global market sizing, opportunity prioritization, a financial business case, and go-to-market strategy.

interviewer_notes: Run the three prompt questions sequentially as mini-cases rather than asking for a traditional framework. Exhibit 1 supports market and vertical prioritization; prompt for qualitative considerations if the candidate gives only a calculation. Exhibit 2 supports the NYC subway P&L and requires careful conversion among billions, millions, thousands, percentages, and per-transaction costs. The $1M past development investment is sunk and excluded from the commercialization decision. The source incorrectly labels fare-collection opportunity results in millions even though Exhibit 1 states annual fare collection in billions.

suggested_framework.summary: Prioritize the expected and timely transit opportunity, build an incremental commercialization P&L, and test strategic benefits and risks before launch.

children.label: Contract win probability and system timing
Brand, strategic fit, and pursuit cost
Annual and cumulative profit, breakeven, and NPV
Proof point for expansion to other cities

stages.interviewer_asks: Using Exhibit 1, which market and transit vertical should PayCo target first?
stages.expected_answer: Prioritize New York subways. Buses have much smaller fare pools and can be screened out quickly. Expected annual subway fare opportunity is $12B x 90% = $10.8B in New York, $13B x 70% = $9.1B in London, and $45B x 20% = $9.0B in Tokyo. New York is highest and is ready in 2012; Tokyo is not ready until 2015. A strong candidate should notice that the source calls these figures millions even though the exhibit units are billions, and should test the sensitive 90% win estimate and pursuit costs.
good_answer_signals: Uses fare pool times contract-win probability
Screens out buses and deprioritizes country macro data
Integrates system timing and qualitative strategic factors

stages.interviewer_asks: What additional factors could change the New York priority?
stages.expected_answer: Assess PayCo's brand and relationships in each city, strategic importance, regulatory and technical integration difficulty, sales and implementation cost, competitive intensity, and sensitivity to win probability. Tokyo would exceed New York at a 25% win probability because $45B x 25% = $11.25B, but its 2015 timing still delays value.
good_answer_signals: Notes that a five-point Tokyo probability increase changes the quantitative ranking
Adds cost and capability considerations absent from the exhibit

stages.interviewer_asks: Using Exhibit 2, build the annual TAP profit forecast for the NYC subway opportunity.
stages.release_when: Provide Exhibit 2 after selecting New York subways.
stages.expected_answer: Revenue equals 0.20% of fare collections plus a $250K annual license fee. Cost equals transactions x $0.005 plus advertising and SG&A. Profit is -$300K in 2011, -$50K in 2012, +$200K in 2013, +$200K in 2014, and +$200K in 2015. The $1M past development investment is sunk and excluded from the forward commercialization P&L.
good_answer_signals: Converts transactions in millions and fare collections in millions consistently
Builds revenue and cost separately for each year

stages.interviewer_asks: Does TAP break even in less than five years, and what is cumulative five-year profit?
stages.expected_answer: Cumulative profit is -$300K after 2011, -$350K after 2012, -$150K after 2013, +$50K after 2014, and +$250K after 2015. TAP therefore breaks even during the fourth year and earns $250K over five years before time value of money. A more complete investment assessment would discount the cash flows.
good_answer_signals: Uses cumulative rather than annual profit for breakeven
Mentions NPV without inventing a discount rate

stages.expected_answer: Proceed with a bid for New York subways, subject to validating the 90% win probability and operating forecasts. The project breaks even in year four and produces $250K over five years, while creating brand, market-share, and expansion benefits. Test transaction and fare forecasts, advertising cost, implementation feasibility, and competitor response; then develop a high-level implementation plan. The absolute profit is modest, so the strategic option value matters.
good_answer_signals: Makes a clear proceed recommendation with conditions
Supports it with breakeven and cumulative profit
Balances modest economics with strategic benefits and risks

exhibits.title: Country and transit-system opportunity data
exhibits.description: Country macro indicators plus subway and bus demand, annual fare collection, system timing, and estimated contract-win probability for New York, London, and Tokyo.
exhibits.key_insight: New York subways have the highest probability-weighted fare pool and earlier implementation timing; Tokyo's much larger pool is offset by a low win probability and delayed system change.

exhibits.title: NYC subway forecast and TAP assumptions
exhibits.description: Five-year transaction, fare-collection, pricing, unit-cost, advertising, and SG&A inputs for the NYC subway commercialization business case.
exhibits.key_insight: Processing revenue and transaction cost scale nearly together, while the license fee covers recurring SG&A and recoups the initial advertising spend over time.

math.question: Which subway market has the highest probability-weighted fare opportunity?
givens: Subway annual fare collection: NYC $12B, London $13B, Tokyo $45B
math.answer: New York subways at $10.8B of probability-weighted annual fare opportunity
math.book_answer_if_different: The book gives the same numerical results, 10.8, 9.1, and 9.0, but labels the fare collections and market opportunities as $MM on the solution page. Exhibit 1 explicitly states annual fare collection in $B, so the corrected units are billions.

math.question: What is annual TAP profit for NYC from 2011 through 2015?
When does TAP break even and what is five-year cumulative profit?
math.answer: Breakeven in year 4; $250K cumulative profit after five years

synthesis: PayCo should pursue New York subways, subject to validating the 90% contract-win estimate and operating assumptions. New York has the highest probability-weighted subway fare pool at $10.8B, not the $10.8M unit shown on the source solution page, and is ready in 2012. The forward TAP P&L breaks even in year four and yields $250K over five years, excluding sunk development cost. Bid discipline, transaction forecasts, advertising cost, technical delivery, and competitor response require diligence; strategic brand and expansion value help justify the modest absolute profit.
what_great_looks_like: Screens buses and macro data before calculating
Combines fare pool, win probability, and timing
Maintains units across billions, millions, thousands, percentages, and per-transaction costs
Flags the source's market-opportunity unit error
common_pitfalls: Choosing Tokyo based only on gross fare collection
Using annual profit instead of cumulative profit for breakeven
Including the $1M sunk development cost in the commercialization decision
Applying 0.20% to transactions rather than fare value
Repeating the source's $MM opportunity label despite Exhibit 1's $B units

extraction.notes: All P&L and breakeven calculations were independently recomputed and match the source. The market-prioritization solution contains a unit error: Exhibit 1 reports annual fare collection in billions, but page 241 labels the 10.8, 9.1, and 9.0 opportunity figures as millions. Correct units are billions. Exhibit tables contain inputs only. Reviewed and accepted by Claude 2026-09-30.
